abstract: |
  Protein and nucleotide foundation models (ESM-2, ESM-C, Evo) are
  increasingly used as backbones for sequence-based drug-resistance
  prediction. Their training corpora are dominated by HIV-1 subtype B
  — the majority subtype in the sequencing-rich global north — while
  the global disease burden is dominated by non-B subtypes (A1, C, D,
  CRF02_AG, others) circulating in sub-Saharan Africa. Any
  foundation-model-based clinical tool inherits this bias, but the
  magnitude of the generalisation gap on HIV-1 *pol* has not been
  systematically measured on a public benchmark under an explicit
  subtype-holdout protocol. We describe such a benchmark, drawn from
  the SAWA surveillance platform's East African cohort (~25 000
  sequences from KE, UG, TZ, RW, BI, ET, 1994–2024), and implement
  two non-foundation-model baselines — k-mer logistic regression and
  per-position one-hot random forest — that ship in seconds on a
  laptop. In this protocol paper we (a) specify two split strategies
  (stratified and subtype-holdout), (b) report baseline performance
  on synthetic ground-truth data at a range of sample sizes, (c)
  preregister the foundation-model comparison to be run against SAWA
  v0.1.0, and (d) describe the failure-mode analysis and
  subtype-stratified fine-tuning that Paper 3 v2 will use to
  characterise and (attempt to) close the gap. Baseline evaluators
  and dataset splitters are unit-tested and CI-benchmarked.

# Introduction

The publicly released weights of ESM-2 [@esm2_2023], ESM-C [@esmc2024],
and Evo [@evo_2024] are trained on protein or nucleotide corpora in
which HIV-1 subtype B is systematically over-represented. Subtype B
accounts for the largest fraction of HIV sequences in UniProt and
GenBank because it dominates in the countries whose surveillance and
research programmes have historically produced the most sequences —
North America and Western Europe — while the global epidemiological
burden is dominated by non-B subtypes: subtype C (Southern Africa,
India), CRF02_AG (West Africa), A1 (East Africa, Eastern Europe),
D (East Africa) [@hemelaar2020]. When a foundation-model-based
resistance predictor is trained on a public corpus and evaluated on
data from a sub-Saharan African clinic, the training distribution
and the deployment distribution differ along the very axis (subtype)
that most affects mutation prevalence, wild-type polymorphism, and
Sierra rule behaviour.

This is not a new observation. Non-B-specific effects on Stanford
HIVdb calls are well documented [@wensing2019]. What has not been
done is a *systematic subtype-holdout benchmark*: train on B, test on
non-B, on a public HIV-1 *pol* corpus, with (i) two non-FM baselines
strong enough to expose whether the FMs add value, (ii) per-drug
per-subtype metrics that let readers see the gap decomposed rather
than pooled, and (iii) a preregistered protocol so that the reported
outcome cannot be reverse-engineered to favour the models under test.

This is a protocol paper. Paper 3 v1 (this document) specifies the
benchmark, reports baseline performance on synthetic ground-truth
data, and preregisters the foundation-model comparison. Paper 3 v2,
appearing after the SAWA v0.1.0 data run and the ESM-2 / Evo
fine-tuning runs, reports the actual gap and the effect of
subtype-stratified fine-tuning as the mitigation candidate.

# Related work

HIV-1 drug-resistance prediction has an extensive history using
classical rule-based systems (Stanford HIVdb [@sierra2019], ANRS,
Rega) and ML approaches [@shafer2015]. Recent work has begun
exploring transformer-based sequence encoders for HIV and related
viruses [@steinegger2019; @rives2021]. Foundation-model benchmarks
in biology broadly (BEND [@marin2024], DeepMSA) tend to report
pooled metrics that hide subgroup gaps. To our knowledge no
published benchmark reports HIV-1 drug-resistance predictor
performance under an explicit subtype-holdout protocol on
sub-Saharan-Africa-first data, which is the specific gap this work
addresses.

The AI-for-Biology community has recently converged on the framing
that "reporting mean performance across a heterogeneous test set is
inadequate for clinical or public-health deployment claims"
[@finlayson2021]. This benchmark operationalises that framing for a
specific, high-stakes case.

# Methods

## Data substrate — SAWA v0.1.0

The benchmark data comes from SAWA v0.1.0 [@sawa_v0_1_0], the
frozen data vintage of the SAWA HIV drug-resistance surveillance
platform:

* `data/interim/dr_results.parquet` — per-(accession, drug) Sierra
  output.
* `data/interim/curated/aligned.parquet` — per-accession curated
  silver Parquet: accession, sequence, subtype, country,
  collection_year.

The adapter `foundation_models/data.py::build_fm_dataset` joins the
two on `accession`, produces a per-(accession, drug) binary label
from Sierra levels (`{high, intermediate} → 1`, `{low, susceptible} → 0`),
and drops accessions with missing subtype or empty sequence. The
resulting frame has columns `{accession, sequence, subtype, country,
collection_year, drug, drug_class, label_binary}`.

## Split strategies

Two split strategies are supported, both deterministic given a seed:

**Stratified split** (baseline, `strategy="stratified"`). 70 / 15 /
15 train / val / test, stratified on `(subtype, drug, label_binary)`
so every subtype × drug × label cell is represented in every split.
This is the *fair-baseline* split: classical models are expected to
do well on it, and it is the split against which claims of "the FM
achieves AUROC X" can be reported without confounding by
distribution shift.

**Subtype-holdout split** (thesis, `strategy="subtype_holdout"`).
Train and validation are drawn from a specified pool of subtypes
(default `("B",)`); the test set contains **all** accessions from
subtypes outside that pool. This is the paper's headline
generalisation test: the FM was trained on data from the same
subtypes as its training distribution and is now asked to predict on
data from subtypes it has under-sampled by construction.

Split determinism, subtype-composition invariants, and
stratification correctness are verified by
`tests/foundation_models/test_data.py` (42 tests, CI-enforced).

## Baselines

Two non-foundation-model baselines are implemented in
`foundation_models/baselines.py`. Both wrap scikit-learn
[@pedregosa2011] (already a project dependency), both provide the
same `fit(seqs, y) → predict_proba(seqs) → predict(seqs, threshold)`
interface, and both scale to the full 25 000-sequence cohort in
seconds on a laptop.

* **K-mer logistic regression** (`KmerLogisticRegression`,
  default `k=3`). Sequences are tokenised into non-overlapping
  k-mers over the nucleotide alphabet; k-mer counts feed an
  L2-regularised logistic regression (`solver="liblinear"`, `C=1.0`,
  `max_iter=500`). The vocabulary is locked at fit time so
  transform-time novel k-mers do not perturb the feature width.
  Rationale: composition-dominant baseline that captures no
  positional information. If a foundation model adds no value over
  this, positional or higher-order structure is not being learned.
* **One-hot random forest** (`OneHotRandomForest`,
  `n_estimators=200`). Sequences must be equal-length (aligned);
  each position becomes a one-hot vector over `alphabet ∪ {OTHER}`
  where the OTHER channel absorbs ambiguity or gap. Rationale:
  positional-signal baseline that captures no cross-position
  interactions beyond depth-1 tree splits. Any foundation model
  claim to model long-range co-evolutionary structure should
  meaningfully beat this baseline; if it does not, the FM's added
  parameters and inference cost are not paying off.

Both baselines are unit-tested for signal recovery on synthetic data
carrying a fixed motif (`AAAAAAAA` at position 20; see
`tests/foundation_models/test_baselines.py`).

## Foundation-model backbones (v2)

The FM comparison is preregistered here and will run in Paper 3 v2:

* **ESM-2** [@esm2_2023] — amino-acid tokenisation from HXB2 *pol*
  translation; fine-tuned classification head on per-drug binary
  resistance. Base checkpoint `esm2_t33_650M_UR50D`. Frozen backbone
  and fully-fine-tuned variants both reported.
* **Evo** [@evo_2024] — nucleotide-native FM; fine-tuned head on the
  same task; base checkpoint `evo-1.5-8k-base`.

The FM adapter modules are stubbed (`foundation_models/models/esm2.py`,
`foundation_models/models/evo.py`) with the training-loop interface
locked but no weights downloaded until the v2 run.

## Metrics {#sec-metrics}

Per (drug × subtype × model) cell:

* **AUROC** — area under the ROC curve.
* **PR-AUC** — area under precision-recall; primary metric for
  rare-mutation cells where prevalence is low.
* **Brier score** — mean squared error of the predicted probability
  against the label.
* **ECE** — expected calibration error at 10 uniform-width bins.

Cells with `n_positive < 5` are omitted from scoring — the
minimum-positives filter is `MIN_POSITIVES_TO_SCORE = 5`,
committed as a module constant and preregistered here.
`per_subtype_metrics(df, prob_col, ...)` returns a Polars metrics
frame ready for the manuscript's figures and tables.
Ranking-metric handling of single-class cells returns `None`
rather than raising, to keep aggregation code simple.

## Bootstrap and uncertainty

Point estimates are supplemented with 500-bootstrap 95 % percentile
intervals; bootstrapping is at the accession level (not row level)
so that per-drug rows sharing an accession are resampled as a
block. Bootstrap seeds derive from the run config hash; two runs on
the same data produce identical CIs.

## Reporting

The primary reporting artifact is a per (drug × subtype × model)
metrics table with CIs; the primary figure is AUROC vs subtype for
each model under both split strategies. A secondary figure reports
the AUROC gap between the training-distribution subtype (B) and the
held-out subtypes for each model. The primary quantitative claim of
Paper 3 v2 is the size of that gap, its bootstrap CI, and whether
subtype-stratified fine-tuning closes it.

# Baseline results on synthetic ground truth

The two baselines are exercised on a synthetic sequence-and-label
generator (`benchmarks/paper3_baselines_synth.py`) that produces up
to 20 000 sequences over three subtypes (`B, A1, C`), inserts a
subtype-shared "true" resistance motif (`AAAAAAAA`) at position 20,
and inserts a subtype-specific decoy motif (`GGGGGGGG`) at position
60 in subtype C only.

At seed 42, per-subtype median AUROC under both split strategies
is:

| `n`    | strategy         | k-mer LR (median AUROC) | one-hot RF (median AUROC) |
|-------:|------------------|------------------------:|--------------------------:|
| 2 000  | stratified       | 0.983                   | 1.000                     |
| 2 000  | subtype-holdout  | 0.970                   | 1.000                     |
| 8 000  | stratified       | 0.984                   | 1.000                     |
| 8 000  | subtype-holdout  | 0.972                   | 1.000                     |
| 20 000 | stratified       | 0.977                   | 1.000                     |
| 20 000 | subtype-holdout  | 0.974                   | 1.000                     |

Both baselines recover the true causal motif; the one-hot RF's
positional features perfectly fit the fixed-position insert, and
the k-mer LR — which throws away positional information — still
achieves > 0.97 median AUROC because the 8-mer signal is strong.
Critically, both baselines *retain the signal under the
subtype-holdout split*: the ~1 % LR degradation from 0.983
(stratified, `n = 2000`) to 0.970 (subtype-holdout, same `n`) is
the noise floor against which fine-tuned FMs should be measured.

Per-subtype cells and full JSON are in
`benchmarks/results/paper3_baselines_synth.json`; the benchmark
runs in CI and blocks merge on regression.

This is the floor that fine-tuned FMs must clear in v2. If an FM
does not exceed the k-mer logistic-regression baseline on the
stratified split, or fails to reduce the subtype-holdout gap
relative to the one-hot random forest, the added FM parameters and
inference cost are not paying off.

# Failure-mode analysis (v2)

The v2 analysis will characterise, for each model, the mutation
classes where FMs remain systematically worse than baselines *even
after subtype-stratified fine-tuning*. Hypotheses to be tested:

* **H1**. FMs underperform baselines on positions where subtype B
  wild-type differs from the tested subtype's wild-type; the FM's
  training distribution treats the deployment-time wild-type as a
  variant.
* **H2**. FMs overperform baselines on positions with
  well-characterised drug-pressure signals across many drugs (e.g.
  M184V) because those positions appear frequently in the training
  corpus regardless of subtype.
* **H3**. Subtype-stratified fine-tuning (curriculum: B, then A1,
  then C, then D) closes the H1 gap more than naive fine-tuning
  across all subtypes at once.

These are preregistered here and will be tested in v2 against the
frozen SAWA v0.1.0 vintage.

# Real-data application (preregistered)

The v2 real-data analysis is preregistered in
`paper3_foundation/preregistration.md`. Summary:

* **Cohort:** SAWA v0.1.0, subtypes `{A1, B, C, D, CRF02_AG}` with
  `n ≥ 500` per subtype (subtypes below this threshold reported in a
  supplement, not the primary comparison).
* **Splits:** both stratified and subtype-holdout, seed-locked.
* **Models:** two baselines (this paper) plus ESM-2 and Evo (frozen
  backbone + fully fine-tuned + subtype-stratified fine-tune).
* **Primary metric:** per-(drug × subtype) AUROC and PR-AUC with
  500-bootstrap 95 % percentile CIs.
* **Primary hypothesis:** under the subtype-holdout split, ESM-2 and
  Evo exhibit an AUROC gap between B (train) and non-B (test) whose
  95 % CI excludes zero. Subtype-stratified fine-tuning reduces the
  gap by ≥ 50 % of its magnitude in the vanilla fine-tune.
* **Multiple testing:** Benjamini–Hochberg FDR at `q = 0.05` across
  the drug × subtype cell grid.

Any deviation between the preregistered analysis and the v2
manuscript will be documented as an exploratory finding and excluded
from the headline claim.

# Discussion

Subtype composition of the training corpus is a form of covariate
shift that is easy to identify structurally but hard to fix with
model architecture alone. The two natural mitigations are (a)
subtype-balanced pre-training corpora, which would require
re-training the FMs and is out of reach for a single lab, and (b)
subtype-stratified fine-tuning, which is within reach and is what
this benchmark's v2 will evaluate. Reporting the *gap* — pre- and
post-fine-tuning — matters more than reporting only the post-tuning
metric: a small gap post-tuning is only informative if the pre-tuning
gap was large. The subtype-holdout split makes this comparison
inspectable.

Two limitations bear noting even at the protocol stage:

* **Sierra-level ground truth is not clinical outcome.** Labels are
  derived from HIVdb rules, not from patient response to therapy.
  This is a benchmark of "how well do you predict what Sierra
  would say," not "how well do you predict clinical failure." The
  clinical-endpoint benchmark requires paired virological outcome
  data and is out of scope for a public-sequence-only paper; it is
  the natural extension in Paper 4 (KEMRI deployment).
* **Non-B is not monolithic.** Aggregating A1, C, D as "non-B" for
  reporting convenience obscures within-non-B heterogeneity; the
  primary reporting is per-subtype, not per-B / non-B, precisely to
  avoid this.

Future work is (i) the v2 FM run against SAWA v0.1.0; (ii)
integration of clinical outcome data via Paper 4 (KEMRI); (iii)
extension to ESM-C and to nucleotide-native alternatives beyond
Evo; (iv) evaluation of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA,
QLoRA) as a cost-controllable subtype-stratification strategy.
